segments.title: Tiger and Queen Elizabeth approaching the fast battleship
segments.body: HMS Tiger was already larger and heavier than the Queen Elizabeth class despite being a battlecruiser. Her original design approached the fast-battleship idea through increasing size and density. The Queen Elizabeth class approached a similar combination through the development of faster battleships. Their overlap makes a Tiger-based battleship a plausible subject for a counterfactual. The comparison concerns the ships as originally designed, before later reconstruction.

evidence.note: Tiger's original size, density and relationship to the fast-battleship idea introduce the hypothetical design.

segments.summary: Tiger's size and protection provide the starting point for a hypothetical Queen Elizabeth built around a battlecruiser hull.

segments.title: Overlapping programmes and different trial requirements
segments.body: Tiger belonged to the 1911-1912 programme, while Queen Elizabeth belonged to the 1912-1913 programme. Tiger was laid down in June 1912 and Queen Elizabeth in October. Queen Elizabeth was launched in October 1913, ahead of Tiger in December. Tiger entered service in October 1914, while Queen Elizabeth followed in December because her advanced fire control and new 15-inch guns required longer trials. Their overlapping construction sets the timing constraint for the hypothetical redesign.

evidence.note: Programme years, laying-down and launch dates, and additional trials for Queen Elizabeth's fire control and 15-inch guns.

segments.summary: Queen Elizabeth was launched before Tiger but needed longer trials for her fire control and new 15-inch guns.

segments.title: Heavier battlecruisers and faster battleships
segments.body: Tiger's design had stabilized before Queen Elizabeth's, despite the projects' overlapping construction. Heavier battlecruisers needed more armour coverage and subdivision to fight other battlecruisers. Faster battleships needed enough speed to stop enemy battlecruisers turning the end of the battle line. These operational demands brought the two types toward a shared balance of speed and protection.

evidence.note: Earlier stabilization of Tiger's design, increasing battlecruiser armour and subdivision, and fast battleships guarding the end of the battle line.

segments.summary: Two British design paths address the danger posed by enemy battlecruisers to the fleet's leading ships.

segments.title: Why cruiser support called for 28 knots
segments.body: In this fleet model, cruising speed is about 18 knots and the battle line accelerates to roughly 21 knots on contact. The cruiser reconnaissance line operates at about 28 knots. Battlecruisers are expected to outrun that line, while fast battleships need to maintain contact so they can support it and reinforce the Grand Fleet's leading echelon against an enemy crossing its T. The tactical rule of thumb gives a three-knot advantage enough margin to control range. Six knots adds freedom to approach and withdraw, including running attacks. A seven-knot advantage provides extra allowance, explaining the 28-knot aim against a 21-knot battle line.

evidence.note: Reconnaissance support, protection of the leading echelon and tactical margins of three, six and seven knots.

segments.summary: A 28-knot reconnaissance line needs fast-battleship support ahead of a battle line accelerating to about 21 knots.

segments.title: Why 24 knots still gave Queen Elizabeth tactical value
segments.body: At about 24 knots, the historical Queen Elizabeth class retained a three-knot advantage over a 21-knot battle line. Its longer-ranged guns and battleship protection complicated attacks by faster, more lightly protected battlecruisers. A 27-knot opponent could influence the range while remaining within the battleship's gun coverage. That combination still served the intended tactical role despite the shortfall from the 28-knot aim. Tiger achieved the higher speed, and her ability to continue fighting after damage at Jutland illustrates the resilience of this heavier battlecruiser design.

evidence.note: The usefulness of 24 knots against a 21-knot battle line, gun-range and protection advantages, and Tiger's continued fighting after damage.

segments.summary: Queen Elizabeth's speed fell short of the stated aim but still offered an advantage over a 21-knot battle line.

segments.title: Interpreting the disputed Super Lion connection
segments.body: A supposed link between Fisher and Churchill's Super Lion idea and Queen Elizabeth is doubtful because the designs share little with Lion. Tiger is the more plausible destination of the idea in this interpretation. Several contemporary projects sought fast ships, making similar language difficult to assign confidently. The identification remains tentative.

evidence.note: The Queen Elizabeth link is disputed and Tiger is proposed tentatively as the likelier referent.

segments.summary: The Super Lion idea raises a question about which contemporary fast-ship project Fisher and Churchill had in mind.

segments.title: Pink Lists as dated snapshots of naval readiness
segments.body: Pink Lists record ships' locations and condition on a specific date. Their precision depends on the reporting and communications available at the time. Assessing them requires those limits to be stated in context. A separate archival source recording the same location or condition provides corroboration. Modern systems require scrutiny too: GPS can be spoofed, so the capacity for greater accuracy does not guarantee an accurate record.

evidence.note: Dated ship-location and readiness records, contemporary communications limits, corroboration and GPS spoofing.

segments.summary: Pink Lists help locate ships and assess their condition, provided their date and reporting limits remain clear.

segments.title: Why ship-design folders can mix several projects
segments.body: Ship-design papers can appear in folders carrying another ship's name. Personal recollections can also combine projects discussed during the same meeting. One Admiralty meeting considered sixty design portfolios over two days, including roughly ten battleship and battlecruiser portfolios. Of those capital-ship portfolios, only two eventually produced a built design. In such a crowded decision process, a passing reference to a fast ship can fit more than one project. Identifying the intended design requires context beyond the folder label.

evidence.note: Archival folder overlap and a multi-portfolio meeting illustrate attribution difficulties.

segments.summary: Mixed folders, meetings and recollections make a design label such as Super Lion difficult to trace.

segments.title: The uncertain claim of a Tiger sister named Leopard
segments.body: Singular references to a Super Lion fit the one-off Tiger more naturally in this interpretation. Alex Clarke has found no archival trace of a second Tiger named Leopard, despite a German historian's claim that one was intended. That finding establishes the limit of his search. HMS Leopard was already a C-class destroyer name in use from 1897 to 1919, although renaming the destroyer would have been possible. A successor carrying the 15-inch guns already under development would have constituted a different class. Jaguar was an available alternative, later used for the J-class destroyer HMS Jaguar, F34, in 1938. A badge already existing during preparations in 1937 prompts speculation about earlier work on that name. Its connection to a previous design remains unknown.

evidence.note: Singular Super Lion wording, the uncorroborated Leopard proposal and limits of the archival search, the occupied destroyer name and the tentative Jaguar badge connection.

segments.summary: Singular Super Lion wording supports a tentative Tiger connection, while the claimed Leopard sister remains uncorroborated.

segments.title: British and German battlecruiser roles
segments.body: Early British battlecruisers followed the commerce-warfare logic of outrunning stronger opponents and outgunning faster ones. German battlecruisers tended to be slightly slower than their British counterparts, with protection and duties closer to those of second-line battleships. They could support the main battle line or provide an additional line when Germany lacked enough battleships to match its likely opponent. Japanese large cruisers had a comparable supporting role. At Jutland, Germany's combined capital-ship force still faced a larger British dreadnought force. Britain's response required battlecruisers capable of fighting the tougher German ships. Tiger belongs to that response.

evidence.note: British commerce-warfare roles and the slower, better-protected German battlecruisers intended to support or supplement the battle line, with a comparable Japanese role.

segments.summary: Different expectations of battle-line support help explain why Britain needed a tougher battlecruiser in Tiger.

segments.title: Tiger's belts and the distribution of hull weight
segments.body: Tiger lacked the deep lower belt used in the battleship comparison. Tiger's armour layout had a thin lower strip of about one inch and a main belt reaching roughly nine inches over selected areas, with four inches forward and aft. Upper protection tapers from six inches to five and four inches in the forward areas discussed. Guns, boilers and turbines were distributed along the hull to manage structural loading and balance. Those arrangements help explain both the design's resilience and the limits of its protection.

evidence.note: Tiger's stated belt thicknesses and machinery distribution are connected to hull loading.

segments.summary: Tiger's armour layout shows how a heavily protected battlecruiser still differed from a battleship.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth's deeper belts and selective protection
segments.body: Queen Elizabeth's belt scheme has six inches of upper protection, a thirteen-inch main belt and an eight-inch lower belt. The lower belt is nearly as thick as Tiger's main belt. The battleship combines that protection with 15-inch guns and more concentrated machinery. Its main belt does not extend completely to both ends. In this interpretation, selective protection in Queen Elizabeth and the R class belongs to an evolution toward all-or-nothing armour, developed further in American schemes. Queen Elizabeth is an intermediate example within that argument.

evidence.note: Belt thicknesses, concentrated machinery, unprotected ends and an interpretation of the development toward all-or-nothing armour.

segments.summary: Queen Elizabeth's lower belt nearly matches Tiger's main belt, while selective coverage points toward a different armour philosophy.

segments.title: Hull shape trades speed against gun stability and manoeuvrability
segments.body: Tiger's longer, sleeker hull favours speed. Queen Elizabeth's fuller form favours stable gunfire and manoeuvrability. The battleship's priorities include a better turning circle. Different operational requirements therefore produced different hulls despite the designs' overlapping development.

evidence.note: The two hull forms are compared for speed, stable gunfire and turning.

segments.summary: Tiger's sleeker hull and Queen Elizabeth's fuller form reflect different priorities in speed, gunfire and turning.

segments.title: Construction volume allowed separate specialized hulls
segments.body: Britain's naval industry was building enough ships to support different designs without requiring a common hull. The volume of work reduced the cost significance of those differences. A large fleet also allowed individual types to specialize in different tasks. Tiger and Queen Elizabeth could therefore retain distinct hull and protection schemes despite being built at almost the same time. Both carried six-inch secondary guns. British practice blended casemate protection into the upper-belt armour, although the two ships still differed substantially in overall protection. Building far fewer ships creates greater pressure to reuse a common hull.

evidence.note: Industrial throughput and fleet size allow specialized hulls, with shared six-inch secondaries and integrated casemate and upper-belt protection.

segments.summary: Britain's construction throughput and large fleet made separate battleship and battlecruiser designs affordable.

segments.title: A common Scharnhorst hull in a diesel-fleet scenario
segments.body: The suggested diesel-fleet scenario uses Scharnhorst hulls for carriers and other capital ships. Building repeated versions of one hull could avoid the yard alterations required for progressively larger Bismarck and H-class designs. That continuity could remove some construction delays. The expected direct effect on Germany's fleet is limited, although responses to the fleet could change. These are proposed scenario effects rather than events in the historical construction programme.

evidence.note: Repeated construction of a common hull could avoid yard alterations and delays required by larger Bismarck and H-class ships.

segments.summary: Repeating a Scharnhorst hull in a diesel-fleet scenario could reduce delays from enlarging German shipyards.

segments.title: French intervention and the Anglo-Japanese alliance
segments.body: The scenario assumes France joins Russia from the beginning of hostilities against Japan. That intervention would activate the Anglo-Japanese alliance and bring Britain into the war on Japan's side. British naval pressure would obstruct coal supply and attempts to send fleets toward Japan. A further speculative branch has Wilhelm II taking the opportunity to attack France and Russia. That German intervention is a possibility layered onto the initial scenario.

evidence.note: French intervention would bring Britain into the war under the alliance, with coal denial and possible German opportunism.

segments.summary: French entry into a hypothetical Russo-Japanese War would widen the conflict through the Anglo-Japanese alliance.

segments.title: A rough three-month delay for the Tiger-based design
segments.body: Basing Queen Elizabeth on Tiger requires the battlecruiser's design to progress further before the battleship design begins. The delay is explicitly a rough estimate. Ten weeks is considered possible if Tiger develops as it did historically. The scenario adopts about three months, approximately thirteen weeks, as a more generous allowance. Later commissioning and strategic consequences depend on that assumption.

evidence.note: The waiting period is estimated at ten to thirteen weeks, with three months adopted.

segments.summary: Using Tiger as the basis requires waiting longer for its design, with roughly thirteen weeks adopted for the scenario.

segments.title: Tiger's dimensions and machinery baseline
segments.body: Tiger is 214.6 metres long, about 27.6 metres in beam and 9.9 metres in draught. Her thirty-nine Babcock and Wilcox boilers operate at 235 psi across five rooms. Four rooms have eight boilers and one has seven. Two Brown-Curtis turbine sets drive four shafts, with an output of 85,000 shaft horsepower. The nominal speed is 28 knots, while trials exceeded 29 knots and approached 30. These dimensions and machinery figures provide the comparison used for the hypothetical design.

evidence.note: Tiger's dimensions, thirty-nine boilers, turbine sets, four shafts, power and trial speed.

segments.summary: Tiger's 39-boiler installation supplies a baseline for judging the proposed battleship's power and space requirements.

segments.title: Why boiler count does not directly determine horsepower
segments.body: Shaft horsepower depends on steam volume, steam pressure and turbine efficiency. More boilers or higher-pressure boilers do not guarantee the same proportional increase in power at the shafts. Less efficient turbines can waste the advantage of a stronger steam supply. The interaction also works in the other direction, because turbine efficiency depends partly on the steam conditions available. Dividing Tiger's stated 85,000 shaft horsepower by thirty-nine boilers produces about 2,200 horsepower per boiler. That figure is a rough comparison tool rather than an independent rating for each boiler.

evidence.note: Steam volume, pressure and turbine efficiency limit direct comparisons of horsepower per boiler.

segments.summary: Steam quantity, pressure and turbine efficiency interact, limiting simple comparisons between boiler numbers.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth's boiler and turbine combinations
segments.body: The historical class is 196.2 metres long and 28 metres in beam. Queen Elizabeth, Valiant and Malaya use twenty-four Babcock and Wilcox boilers, while Warspite and Barham use twenty-four Yarrow boilers. Their nominal pressure is 235 psi, with six boilers in each of four rooms. British battleships commonly use this arrangement, while battlecruisers favour eight boilers per room and may have five rooms. SS Imperator uses the same Yarrow boiler type rated at 265 psi. Queen Elizabeth, Warspite and Malaya have the more efficient Parsons turbine sets, with cruising units for improved fuel economy; Barham and Valiant have Brown-Curtis sets. The intended output is 75,000 shaft horsepower, giving a rough comparison above 3,000 horsepower per boiler. Barham is the slowest example, producing less than 71,000 shaft horsepower at deep load and reaching 23.9 knots on trials, against a class average near 24 knots.

evidence.note: Ship-specific machinery, British boiler-room conventions, Imperator's higher boiler pressure, intended output and Barham's trial performance.

segments.summary: Different boiler and turbine combinations help explain why twenty-four boilers could support a high power target.

segments.title: An unpublished hypothesis about Warspite's steam surges
segments.body: Warspite combines Yarrow boilers with Parsons turbines, unlike the slower Barham. A Royal Navy engineer's unpublished hypothesis links her occasional extra speed to boilers capable of a higher operating level, with uneven settings causing steam surges. Those surges would explain intermittent bursts of power above her sisters. The engineer died before publishing the book, and Alex Clarke read manuscript sections shared by the engineer's family through their connection with his father. The mechanism remains an unpublished hypothesis. Later Brown-Curtis turbine designs became more efficient, including the generation fitted to Hood.

evidence.note: Unpublished engineer's hypothesis linking uneven boiler operation to steam surges and extra speed, with family-supplied manuscript testimony and later Hood-era turbine development.

segments.summary: An unpublished naval engineer's hypothesis links Warspite's performance differences to uneven boiler settings and steam surges.

segments.title: Lion and Iron Duke as machinery comparisons
segments.body: A 265-psi boiler option is available for the proposed machinery. Lion is 213.4 metres long, 27 metres in beam and 9.9 metres in draught, with forty-two earlier Yarrow boilers and Parsons turbines producing 70,000 shaft horsepower through four shafts. Her boilers occupy six rooms of seven. The class's nominal speed is 27 knots, while Princess Royal reached 28.5 knots on trials. Iron Duke is 189.8 metres long, 27.4 metres in beam and 9.98 metres in draught. Its eighteen Babcock and Wilcox or Yarrow boilers supply four Parsons turbines, producing 29,000 shaft horsepower for about 21.25 knots. These installations show how boiler-room arrangements, pressure and turbine efficiency were changing during the design period.

evidence.note: Lion's six rooms of seven boilers, Princess Royal's trial speed, Iron Duke's installation and the higher-pressure boiler option.

segments.summary: Earlier battlecruiser and battleship installations show how rapidly machinery options were changing.

segments.title: Higher steam pressure and turbine blade efficiency
segments.body: Raising boiler pressure from 235 to 265 psi is an increase of about thirteen percent. The estimate treats that as a roughly thirteen-percent power boost for the proposed machinery. More efficient turbines would make better use of the steam supply. Parsons' efficiency advantage comes from blade design. The power percentage is a simplifying assumption in the estimate.

evidence.note: A thirty-psi increase treated as a thirteen-percent power boost, alongside the efficiency advantage of Parsons turbine blades.

segments.summary: The machinery estimate treats a rise from 235 to 265 psi as a roughly thirteen-percent power boost, with turbine blade design offering another efficiency gain.

segments.title: Hull proportions and the yards that could build them
segments.body: The length-to-beam ratios are 7.78 for Tiger, 7.01 for historical Queen Elizabeth, 7.66 for the proposed ship, 7.9 for Lion and 6.93 for Iron Duke. The historical battleship hull follows the Iron Duke design line in this interpretation. Adopting Tiger's longer form offers a different route toward efficient speed. The proposed length is 24.8 metres greater than Iron Duke's, while remaining below Hood's size. Yards capable of building Tiger should therefore be able to accommodate this version of Queen Elizabeth. A finer hull supports the feasibility of greater speed, although the ratio alone cannot establish the final performance.

evidence.note: A proposed 7.66 length-to-beam ratio and a hull that yards already capable of building Tiger could accommodate.

segments.summary: Length-to-beam ratios explain the proposed gain in speed efficiency and its compatibility with existing yards.

segments.title: Battleship armour constrains boiler-room space
segments.body: The hypothetical battleship cannot simply retain Tiger's full boiler-room arrangement. Heavier armour requires hull framing and subdivision able to carry the additional weight. That support consumes space that might otherwise be assigned to machinery. Armour and machinery must therefore be planned together in the longer hull.

evidence.note: Hull framing and subdivision needed to support heavier armour consume space otherwise available for machinery.

segments.summary: Supporting heavier armour requires framing and subdivision that prevent a direct copy of Tiger's five boiler rooms.

segments.title: Thirty-two boilers and Parsons turbines
segments.body: The proposed installation has thirty-two Yarrow boilers at 265 psi, arranged in four rooms of eight. Tiger supplies the hull basis, while Parsons turbines replace Tiger's original machinery combination. The intended output is roughly 80,000-85,000 shaft horsepower. A comparison figure of 2,500 horsepower per boiler would produce 80,000 horsepower from thirty-two boilers. That sits between the rough Tiger figure and the higher target used for historical Queen Elizabeth. It is a plausibility estimate rather than a completed machinery design.

evidence.note: Four rooms of eight 265-psi Yarrow boilers and a rough 2,500-horsepower-per-boiler assumption yield an 80,000-horsepower starting estimate.

segments.summary: The proposed machinery combines four rooms of eight Yarrow boilers with Parsons turbines and an estimated 80,000-85,000 shaft horsepower.

segments.title: A provisional armour and turret arrangement
segments.body: The proposed armour arrangement might move further toward selective all-or-nothing protection. It retains a thirteen-inch main belt and an eight-inch lower belt, with possible reductions in forward coverage. Two funnels could remain, as in the historical class. The longer hull also offers the possibility of moving one aft 15-inch turret toward a Q position resembling Tiger's arrangement. These are provisional choices for balancing machinery, armament and weight. They do not establish a settled layout.

evidence.note: Potential belt coverage, funnels and turret relocation are explicitly tentative.

segments.summary: The longer ship could retain heavy belts and two funnels while changing the position of an aft turret.

segments.title: Could extra time help the longer 15-inch gun?
segments.body: The assumed delay gives the gun programme a little more development time. A working 15-inch/45 might reduce the pressure to adopt the shorter 15-inch/42, developed by adapting the earlier 13.5-inch/45 design. Three extra months might help resolve the difficulties, although a substantial change remains doubtful. A parallel larger-calibre programme is associated with the gun first proposed for G3 and is distinguished from Nelson's later 16-inch weapon. The Nelson gun belongs to a later design shaped by conclusions drawn from captured German ships and guns. Those tests are judged insufficient to prove the underlying ideas.

evidence.note: Extra development time is considered cautiously, with the G3-era programme distinguished from Nelson's later gun.

segments.summary: Three extra months might help the 15-inch/45 programme, although a major change in gun development remains doubtful.

segments.title: Keeping battleship beam on Tiger's longer hull
segments.body: The estimated length is about 214.6 metres, with 215 metres also considered possible. The ship still needs at least 28 metres of beam for the 15-inch armament. It is therefore slightly broader than Tiger while retaining the battlecruiser's approximate length. Those dimensions produce the stated length-to-beam ratio of about 7.66. The proposal gains a longer hull without narrowing the battleship to Tiger's beam.

evidence.note: The estimated length and minimum beam explain the proposed ratio.

segments.summary: The proposed ship retains at least 28 metres of beam for its 15-inch guns while adopting Tiger's approximate length.

segments.title: Delayed entry, Gallipoli and Jutland availability
segments.body: The three-month shift places Queen Elizabeth's entry in March 1915 and Warspite's in June 1915. The remaining dates used in the scenario are January 1916 for Barham, April for Valiant and May for Malaya. Queen Elizabeth could consequently miss the Gallipoli operation. Tiger or Dreadnought is suggested as a possible replacement flagship. Dreadnought already has flagship fittings and is not considered essential to the Grand Fleet in this scenario. Four Queen Elizabeths would probably still be available for Jutland. These dates and deployments are consequences of the assumed delay.

evidence.note: Scenario commissioning dates are connected to possible Gallipoli deployment and Jutland availability.

segments.summary: The assumed delay could keep Queen Elizabeth away from Gallipoli while leaving four sisters available for Jutland.

segments.title: The unresolved design of the proposed sixth Queen Elizabeth
segments.body: The unbuilt sixth Queen Elizabeth, Agincourt, has an uncertain design history. One reconstruction envisages six 18-inch guns in three twin turrets, drawing on an 18-inch gun programme already under development and work on twin mountings. Three larger turrets might release space for extra boilers compared with a four-turret ship, while higher boiler pressure could support an estimated 27-28 knots. The precise design remains unresolved in this reconstruction, with research into the design continuing. In the Tiger-based scenario, the five other ships would already be fast battleships. Agincourt might therefore be completed to their common design without the separate 18-inch armament, giving the fleet a sixth ship.

evidence.note: The active 18-inch programme and twin-mounting work support a tentative six-gun reconstruction, with possible extra boiler space and an alternative common-design completion.

segments.summary: The unbuilt Agincourt raises competing possibilities: a distinctive six-gun fast battleship or another ship of the common class design.

segments.title: Why the estimate rounds up to 30,000 tons
segments.body: The proposed standard displacement is rounded to 30,000 tons. That is about 1,500 tons above Tiger, 2,500 above historical Queen Elizabeth and 5,000 above Iron Duke. Repeated calculations using published weight figures produce estimates from about 29,000 to 29,500 tons. An allowance of roughly 500 tons is added because some weight might have been missed. The result is a cautious estimate rather than an exact design total. It remains well below the approximately 42,000-ton Hood comparison and is considered within British construction capacity.

evidence.note: Repeated calculations and an uncertainty allowance explain the rounded standard-displacement estimate.

segments.summary: Repeated weight estimates produce figures below 30,000 tons, with an added margin for potentially missed items.

segments.title: Higher speed with battleship-like acceleration
segments.body: The rough estimate treats each higher-pressure boiler as about thirteen percent more capable than Tiger's boilers, giving thirty-two boilers approximately the output of thirty-six older ones. Parsons turbines and cruising units provide another expected efficiency advantage over Tiger's installation. The proposed machinery is expected to produce roughly 80,000-85,000 shaft horsepower. Higher output could require accepting greater machinery wear, as in the operation of the historical Queen Elizabeth class. Added weight is expected to affect acceleration particularly strongly. The longer, finer hull helps sustain speed, although the ship still accelerates like a battleship. Its greater size also makes it a larger target requiring armour over a longer hull. In this assessment, the resulting ship would probably be a better fit for Second World War duties than the historical class.

evidence.note: Power, machinery wear, acceleration, finer hull shape and target size are weighed together.

segments.summary: Higher-pressure boilers and a finer hull offer greater speed, while added weight leaves the ship with battleship-like acceleration.

segments.title: Fuel load, full displacement and Suez access
segments.body: Standard displacement and full-load displacement are kept separate in the estimate. Tiger's stated fuel allowance is about 3,900 tons of oil and 3,400 tons of coal. The hypothetical battleships are expected to carry less, with around 5,000 tons suggested as a typical battleship fuel allowance. Adding fuel, water and other supplies gives a tentative full-load estimate near 37,000-38,000 tons. The proposed beam remains 28 metres, matching the historical class. With its unchanged beam, the longer ship should still be able to pass through the Suez Canal.

evidence.note: Fuel allowances, approximate full load and unchanged beam support the canal-access assessment.

segments.summary: The 30,000-ton estimate excludes fuel and water, which could bring full load to roughly 37,000-38,000 tons.

segments.title: The proposed 28-knot speed remains uncertain
segments.body: The design aims for the greatest speed achievable from a Tiger-based hull with battleship protection. Reaching 28 knots remains uncertain, although that result would not be surprising within the assumptions. Thirty-two boilers occupy four rooms of eight, compared with Tiger's thirty-nine boilers. Its appearance could combine features of Tiger and Queen Elizabeth. Balancing weight and displacement might require the aft Y turret to become a Q turret, while secondary fire-control or mast positions could also change. No completed SpringSharp or Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts model accompanies these estimates, so neither the layout nor the top speed is established.

evidence.note: Uncertain top speed, four rooms of eight boilers, possible Y-to-Q turret relocation and the absence of a completed design model.

segments.summary: The final design assessment leaves top speed and some turret, mast and fire-control positions provisional.

segments.title: Making the German naval race financially unsustainable
segments.body: In this interpretation, Britain could end naval competition by making Germany's next building programme too expensive. Once naval expenditure required money from the army's budget, the army would resist further expansion. Faster, heavily armed Queen Elizabeths could force Germany out of the competition earlier, without requiring the further shock of Britain ordering eight R-class ships before Germany had a 15-inch-gun battleship. An earlier version of the same strategy imagines Britain announcing eight Dreadnoughts immediately. The Royal Navy understood the financial mechanism, but the historical government did not supply the funding and political support needed to pursue it on that scale.

evidence.note: Army-budget resistance as a proposed limit on German naval expansion, the comparison with eight R-class orders before Germany has a 15-inch-gun ship, and the unrealized option of ordering eight Dreadnoughts immediately.

segments.summary: A major British capability increase could intensify the budget pressure between Germany's navy and army.

segments.title: American standard battleships facing a faster opponent
segments.body: American standard battleships operating at 21 knots would face a substantial disadvantage against British battleships making 27-28 knots. Larger guns would still leave the faster opponent considerable control over where and how to engage. One possible response is raising American battle-line speed to about 25 knots; adoption of the full British speed remains uncertain. The US Navy could press for that change while members of Congress argued that an enemy must approach the slower fleet to fight it. That hypothetical congressional objection overlooks the slower fleet's inability to compel an engagement on its preferred terms.

evidence.note: A possible American move toward 25 knots and the hypothetical disagreement over whether a slower fleet can determine engagement conditions.

segments.summary: British battleships making 27-28 knots would challenge American standardization around a 21-knot battle line.

segments.title: Changing bearing and range with superior speed
segments.body: A faster fleet can change angle, bearing and distance more freely than a slower opponent. Those changes complicate the opponent's firing problem. Completely circling a 21-knot fleet with a 27-28-knot force is offered as a theoretical illustration. Practical sea conditions make that manoeuvre unlikely. S curves ahead of the opposing battle line provide the more plausible example of exploiting the speed difference.

evidence.note: Changing angle, bearing and distance complicates gunnery, with S curves a more practical example than completely circling the opposing fleet.

segments.summary: A faster force can complicate gunnery by changing its bearing and range, even when a complete encirclement is impractical.

segments.title: A speculative building pause and delayed First World War
segments.body: The modified Queen Elizabeth class could make other powers pause and reconsider their construction plans, producing another design shock comparable to Dreadnought. Governments redeveloping their forces might then be less willing to escalate a crisis. In that speculative branch, the assassination still occurs, but the wider war is delayed. A twelve-month pause elsewhere, set against the British three-month redesign delay, would give Britain a net nine-month advantage in this example. More British ships could therefore finish in peacetime or be close to completion when hostilities began.

evidence.note: A proposed foreign construction pause, possible reluctance to escalate a crisis and the conditional nine-month British timetable advantage.

segments.summary: A second Dreadnought-like design shock could prompt reassessment, with a further speculative effect on readiness for war.

segments.title: Keeping Agincourt within the fast Queen Elizabeth design
segments.body: In this branch, the proposed Agincourt already belongs to a Queen Elizabeth design approaching 28 knots. A separate six-18-inch-gun version would therefore offer little speed advantage. The longer hull gives more space for those weapons, but the priority could be increasing the number of ships able to perform the new fast-battleship role. Continuing the common class design would provide another pace-setting ship without requiring that distinctive armament.

evidence.note: The proposed sixth ship has little speed incentive for six 18-inch guns, while increasing fast-battleship numbers could favour continuing the common design.

segments.summary: A sixth fast Queen Elizabeth could take priority over a special Agincourt carrying six 18-inch guns.

segments.title: A cheaper R class that preserves speed
segments.body: Three triple 15-inch turrets, with two forward and one aft, offer a possible R-class economy that preserves speed. The ships' length and beam could make that arrangement preferable to saving money by accepting a slower battle line. The scenario could repeat a procurement compromise: the navy wants six ships, the Treasury wants two, and four are agreed with four more if circumstances require them. Eight R-class ships were ordered, while five were built historically. If the war began later and construction were further advanced, all eight could potentially be completed. Together with six Queen Elizabeths, that would yield fourteen battleships. Their speed remains conditional on the design branch adopted; the R class could retain its historical emphasis on a cheaper battle-line ship or pursue greater capability. Its historical armour arrangement is judged better than Queen Elizabeth's in this comparison.

evidence.note: Three triple turrets as an economy preserving speed, the eight-ship procurement sequence and conditional completion of fourteen battleships across both classes.

segments.summary: Three triple turrets offer a possible way to reduce cost while keeping a fast battle line.

segments.title: Italian fast-battleship ambitions and British throughput
segments.body: Britain reaching a 28-knot battleship ahead of the Francesco Caracciolo programme would frustrate Italian fast-battleship ambitions. In the imagined response, criticism falls on Italian funding and slow decisions. Britain has the advantage of an established production flow and a much larger volume of battleship construction. If rival powers paused while Britain continued building, Britain could recover part of the numerical advantage lost through the Dreadnought transition. Any wider delay in the outbreak of war could also benefit France and other powers, although that remains a separate speculative consequence.

evidence.note: Italian fast-battleship ambitions, British production volume and the conditional advantage from continued building during foreign pauses.

segments.summary: British production volume could turn the design advantage into completed ships before rival programmes.

segments.title: Fast Queen Elizabeths in Jutland's run to the south
segments.body: If war begins on the historical schedule, the modified Queen Elizabeths could fight at the front of Jutland's run to the south instead of lagging behind the battlecruisers. In this assessment, they bring probably the best battleship fire control then available and the most powerful battleship guns available for combat service. Their 15-inch armament would add heavy firepower to the British force. The added battleships also give the German ships more targets over which to disperse their fire. Those targets have battleship protection and are designed to withstand heavier punishment. British losses might therefore fall, while German losses are expected to increase. These outcomes depend on the faster ships reaching and sustaining their place in the counterfactual action.

evidence.note: Projected fire-control superiority, 15-inch gun power and additional armoured targets during the run to the south.

segments.summary: Faster battleships could join the front of the action, adding heavy firepower and protected targets to the British force.

segments.title: A damaged scouting force could change Scheer's decision
segments.body: The scenario imagines the High Seas Fleet arriving after the First Scouting Group has been reduced to one or two capital ships remaining in the fight, or possibly none. Under those conditions, Scheer would probably withdraw. A British force making 27-28 knots could escape before the slower German battle fleet caught it. If the British instead maintained a speed just low enough to preserve contact, that deliberate restraint would warn of an attempt to lead the pursuers toward Jellicoe. The judgment assumes Scheer would recognize that danger. The scale of the scouting-force losses and his eventual decision remain counterfactual outcomes.

evidence.note: Severe hypothetical First Scouting Group losses, British freedom to escape and deliberately limited speed as a warning of a trap.

segments.summary: Severe damage to the German scouting force could encourage withdrawal, while British speed makes a pursuit hazardous.

segments.title: Competing demands on fast battleships and gunnery training
segments.body: The modified ships are attractive reinforcements for the battlecruiser force, making it harder for Jellicoe to retain them with the Grand Fleet. Their intended role is to protect the battle fleet and prevent an enemy crossing its T. The battlecruiser force also lacks sufficient space for gunnery practice. In this critical assessment, Beatty's rank and influence should have allowed him to secure better arrangements earlier, and practice away from his influence would be preferable. His acceptance of the existing situation left Jellicoe to intervene. The new fast battleships would therefore face competing deployment demands even while the training problem remained.

evidence.note: Grand Fleet protection competes with battlecruiser reinforcement, alongside criticism of Beatty's handling of gunnery practice.

segments.summary: Ships well suited to protecting the Grand Fleet could become difficult to retain there when the battlecruiser force needs reinforcement.

segments.title: Fast battleships weaken the case for battlecruiser successors
segments.body: An established fast-battleship class would change the case for ordering the historical Admiral class. If the R class already retains high speed, perhaps through triple 15-inch turrets that reduce cost, Fisher could no longer justify cancelling those battleships and turning them into battlecruisers on speed grounds alone. His large light cruisers could face stronger resistance for similar reasons. A request for 32 knots would have to justify the extra speed against the protection already available in the fast battleships. Fisher's freedom of action would narrow, and further fast battleships become the expected successor path.

evidence.note: Fast R-class battleships would weaken Fisher's conversion argument and require a stronger justification for a 32-knot alternative.

segments.summary: An established fast battle line could limit Fisher's arguments for replacing battleships with battlecruisers.

segments.title: A twelve-gun fast battleship successor
segments.body: If the R class establishes triple 15-inch turrets, its successor could carry twelve guns. The imagined ship is designed for at least 28 knots, with 28-30 knots used in the later estimate. Standard displacement is about 45,000 tons, possibly more. Its speed and battleship protection are expected to make a post-Jutland construction pause or extensive redesign unnecessary. It could continue through construction and enter service while filling gaps in the fleet. These are hypothetical specifications, without a completed historical design.

evidence.note: A twelve-15-inch-gun successor at 28-30 knots and roughly 45,000 tons standard, expected to continue through construction after Jutland.

segments.summary: The triple-turret branch leads to an imagined successor with twelve 15-inch guns, about 45,000 tons and 28-30 knots.

segments.title: A fast battle line changes treaty bargaining
segments.body: At the upper end of the scenario, fourteen ships carry eight or nine 15-inch guns and make roughly 28 knots, while four successors carry twelve 15-inch guns and reach about 30 knots. That would place eighteen fast capital ships in the British fleet by the treaty period. The historical Hood, at approximately 42,000 tons in this comparison, could be treated as a single exception. Four approximately 45,000-ton fast battleships would be harder to accommodate under a 35,000-ton standard-displacement limit. Their battleship protection and greater gun power would also change comparisons with the American Colorado class. A ship-for-ship equivalence could therefore become contentious, alongside the displacement limit. The treaty terms remain uncertain.

evidence.note: The upper-end eighteen-ship fleet, the single 42,000-ton Hood exception and disputes over 45,000-ton classes and Colorado equivalence.

segments.summary: Four 45,000-ton fast battleships would make a 35,000-ton limit harder to negotiate than a single exceptional Hood.

segments.title: Would Amagi and Lexington still be battlecruisers?
segments.body: An earlier British fast-battleship line could alter later foreign procurement. Amagi and Lexington might be laid down at a different time or emerge in a different form. Other navies could order protected fast battleships in place of the historical battlecruiser designs. The timing and replacement specifications remain open; no particular alternative is established.

evidence.note: Uncertain effects on the timing and form of Amagi and Lexington, including a possible turn toward fast battleships.

segments.summary: An earlier British fast-battleship line raises uncertainty about the form of later Japanese and American ships.

segments.title: Eight or nine 16.5-inch guns in the successor class
segments.body: Larger-gun branches replace the twelve 15-inch guns with eight 16.5-inch guns in twin turrets or nine in three triple turrets. These hypothetical successors retain roughly 30 knots and battleship protection at about 45,000 tons standard displacement. That is approximately 15,000 tons more than even the modified Queen Elizabeth in this comparison. Other navies would have to assess whether their existing designs could match such a combination of gun power, speed and protection. The nine-gun branch would increase the armament further while preserving the same general design aims.

evidence.note: Eight- and nine-16.5-inch-gun branches at roughly 30 knots and 45,000 tons standard, around 15,000 tons larger than the modified Queen Elizabeth.

segments.summary: Larger-gun branches preserve the proposed speed and protection while increasing pressure on rival designs.

segments.title: Why Tiger and Queen Elizabeth remained separate designs
segments.body: One explanation for the historical separation is that Queen Elizabeths were already being produced as quickly as possible. Tiger and Queen Elizabeth were also considered as separate design projects. Combining their attributes would have required someone to pose that design question while accepting a change to the timetable. In the closing interpretation, the pressure to build quickly and the separation of the design discussions explain why that combination was never pursued.

evidence.note: Construction urgency and separate consideration of the two designs as the closing explanation for their historical separation.

segments.summary: Construction urgency and separate design discussions help explain why Tiger's hull was never combined with Queen Elizabeth's attributes.
